item.title: Pacific Islands
item.description: Pacific nations are pushing for stronger regional cooperation and sustainable early warning systems as climate-related hazards continue to threaten communities across the region. The issues were highlighted at the Eighth Meeting of the Pacific Meteorological Council was officially opened at the Fa'onelua centre in Nuku'alofa today.
item.content:encoded:
Pacific nations are pushing for stronger regional cooperation and sustainable early warning systems as climate-related hazards continue to threaten communities across the region.

The issues were highlighted at the Eighth Meeting of the Pacific Meteorological Council was officially opened at the Fa'onelua centre in Nuku'alofa today.

Delivering the keynote address, Dr Viliami Latu said Pacific countries needed to ensure investments in meteorological and disaster infrastructure could be maintained long after development projects ended. He asked delegates to consider who would maintain weather and early warning systems five, 10 and 20 years after the projects that funded them had ended.

“An early warning system that cannot be maintained will eventually cease to be an early warning system,” he said.

Dr Latu said maintenance, replacement, insurance, lifecycle costs, national capacity and sustainable financing needed to be considered from the beginning of every investment.

“This is not simply a technical issue, it is a question of Pacific resilience, development and security.”

World Meteorological Organization Regional Office Director Ishaam Abader said strengthening meteorological services was ultimately about protecting Pacific communities.

“Strengthening weather, climate and water services is not only about science and technology,” Abader said.

“It is more importantly about protecting lives, supporting sustainable development, safeguarding livelihoods and enhancing resilience across Pacific communities.”

Dr Latu said future partnerships with development partners must ensure systems built with external support could eventually be operated, maintained and sustained by Pacific nations.

He said new satellite technology, forecasting systems and artificial intelligence would strengthen meteorological services, but technology alone would not make the Pacific “Weather Ready”.

“The most important investment we can make remains an investment in our people,” he said.

Dr Latu highlighted the role of meteorologists, hydrologists, technicians, observers, forecasters, disaster managers, communicators and communities in building resilience.

He also stressed regional cooperation, saying weather systems and natural hazards did not recognise national borders.

Pacific nations needed to continue sharing knowledge, observations, technology, expertise and resources while developing systems that reflected regional priorities, he said.

Dr Latu said the Pacific Meteorological Council provided an important platform for that collective work.

He challenged delegates to consider whether decisions made at the meeting would ultimately make Pacific communities safer.

“If the answer is yes, then our work is worthwhile,” he said.

Dr Latu said Pacific communities could combine traditional knowledge of the environment with modern science and technology to better understand and respond to hazards.

He said the goal should be a Pacific where communities understood the risks they faced, received warnings in time and could act before hazards became tragedies.

“That is the Pacific we should seek to build,” he said.

“A Pacific that is informed. A Pacific that is prepared. A Pacific whose systems are sustainable. And ultimately, a Pacific that is ‘Secure’.”

Priest jailed for dangerous driving that caused passenger's death
item.description: Ha'unga Junior Tupou (41) is serving one year and ten months imprisonment for dangerous driving after a drinking spree, which caused the death of his passenger, when he drove in excessive speed towards Tokomololo, lost control of the vehicle which swerved and struck a fence. Hon. Justice Targowski KC sentenced him on 24 August at the Supreme Court in Nuku’alofa, after he pleaded guilty.
item.content:encoded:
Ha'unga Junior Tupou (41) is serving one year and ten months imprisonment for dangerous driving after a drinking spree, which caused the death of his passenger, when he drove in excessive speed towards Tokomololo, lost control of the vehicle which swerved and struck a fence.

Hon. Justice Targowski KC sentenced him on 24 August at the Supreme Court in Nuku’alofa, after he pleaded guilty.

The offending was on 20 January this year, when the defendant and the deceased Salesi Hopo, who was a close friend, and others had spent the afternoon drinking kava and wine at Veitongo. The defendant, the deceased and a third man, 'Alipate Ngata& went to Billfish Bar in Nuku'alofa to continue drinking. At around midnight, the defendant and his companions left the bar.

The judge stated that the defendant then drove with 'Alipate as his front-seat passenger and the deceased seated behind him. 'Alipate fell asleep. The defendant drove at excessive speed, and his manner of driving woke 'Alipate, when the vehicle crossed a speed hump near Lavengamalie College. 'Alipate asked him to slow down.

The defendant ignored that warning and continued at speed. At the junction at Tofoa, the vehicle veered onto the wrong side of the road. Then at Pea, the defendant made a sharp right turn and narrowly avoided striking a stone wall. He continued at speed towards Tokomololo and failed to stop at a four-way intersection. He continued driving very fast and eventually lost control of the vehicle.

The& vehicle swerved to the right side of the road and struck a fence bounding a residence. The impact of the collision caused the vehicle to flip onto its side. Although spoken to by witnesses who arrived at the scene shortly after the accident, the defendant did not remain at the scene. He left before the police arrived.

The deceased suffered a severe head injury and died at Vaiola Hospital at around 7 am the& following morning. The defendant was arrested later and cooperated with the police. He had no previous convictions, stated the judge.

The deceased was a good and close personal friend of the defendant who is a Catholic priest.

In addition to a Pre-Sentence Report, the defendant produced to the court excellent character references. Pending the outcome of this case, the defendant had been placed on administrative leave from all duties and public ministry by his church, stated the judge.

The consequences of the defendant's irresponsible behaviour had far-reaching social and personal repercussions

“His vocation does not entitle him to be sentenced differently from any other person. ...The death of Salesi Hopo will live with the deceased's family for years to come."

The judge took into account the fact that the defendant cooperated with the police after his arrest, his remorse and the personal effect on his life that he will continue to bear.

After having regard to the character reference, together with his remorse and cooperation, the judge reduced the starting point by 18 months to five years and six months' imprisonment.

“The death of Salesi Hopo is an essential element of the offence. It is not to be treated as a separate aggravating factor. It does, however, represent the irreversible harm resulting from the defendant's conduct. This was not a momentary error of judgment. The defendant persisted in driving dangerously over some distance. He drove at speed, narrowly avoided an earlier collision, failed to stop at an intersection and ignored an express warning from his passenger. He had several opportunities to consider the consequences of his behaviour and bring his driving under control but failed to do so."

The defendant had consumed alcohol over a considerable period of hours before the accident. The reason no blood-alcohol reading was produced in evidence is because he did not remain at the scene.

For the defendant's guilty plea at the first reasonable opportunity, the judge allowed a 30 percent discount. Applying that and rounding the result in his favour resulted in a sentence of three years and ten months' imprisonment. Two years was then suspended for two years on conditions that he must not commit any imprisonable offence, during the suspension period.

He must undertake any alcohol-awareness, road-safety or other rehabilitative counselling directed by the Probation Office, with his driver's license to be disqualified/prohibited from obtaining one for four-years, after release.

The defendant is now serving one year and ten months in prison.

item.content:encoded:
Global temperature rise is set to cross 1.5°C, likely within the next few years, pushing climate risks and impacts to increasingly dangerous heights, but it is still possible to bring temperatures down and achieve global goals in the Paris Agreement, according to a new United Nations Environment Programme ( UNEP ) report. Anticipated impacts include intensified extreme weather, ecosystem loss, and submersion of Small Island Developing States and low-lying coastal cities.

The report, ‘ Limiting Overshoot ’, identifies an ‘overshoot, peak, and decline’ pathway as the best remaining option to minimize the magnitude and duration of this overshoot and try to return to below 1.5°C as soon as possible.

“This summer’s scorching heat, raging wildfires and deadly floods are a warning of what lies ahead. We must make the overshoot above 1.5 degrees as small and short as possible. That demands an overshoot of ambition” said UN Secretary-General Antőnio Guterres.

This pathway would minimize peak temperature rise through immediate and sustained cuts to greenhouse gas emissions, including methane, on the road to net-zero, and bring down temperatures through long-term net-negative emissions, with carefully governed Carbon Dioxide Removal ( CDR ) – the process of removing carbon from the air and storing it through afforestation or other means – an essential part of the mix.

At the same time, following this pathway would involve adaptation actions that reduce vulnerability to the current, expected and unexpected impacts of climate change on societies, communities and economies – although there will likely be limits to adaptation and irreversible impacts, especially if peak temperatures are not minimized. The report stresses such a pathway would reduce risks and impacts, make adaptation less difficult and expensive, and increase the chances of lowering temperatures.

“There are no good outcomes if we remain above 1.5°C. Across the globe, extreme heatwaves are already proving that climate impacts will strike faster, hit harder, and last longer - costing more lives and causing deeper disruption,” said Inger Andersen, Executive Director of UNEP . “Now is the time we must double down on climate action. We can – and must – get on the right path. By cutting greenhouse gas emissions, strengthening resilience and adaptation, and ensuring exceedance of 1.5°C is as small and short as possible.”

The most optimistic scenario will see temperature rise peak at 1.8°C above pre-industrial levels, above the goal of limiting warming to 1.5°C set by the Paris Agreement. Most other scenarios predict higher peaks.

Above 1.5°C, risks and impacts will intensify with every extra fraction of a degree and every year. Severe damage to human health, food security, water supplies, nature, cities, infrastructure, and economies is expected.

The report warns that the likelihood of crossing irreversible tipping points increases with the magnitude and duration of higher temperatures. These include the destabilization of major ice sheets, degradation of the Amazon rainforest and disruption of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (the system of currents that moves warm surface water north and cold deep water south, playing a key role in regulating the climate). Some impacts may emerge abruptly, while others will accumulate over time.

Considering the scale of the risks and the co-benefits of climate interventions such as a rapid transition away from fossil fuels to renewable energy – improving air quality and public health, lowering energy costs and increasing access to electricity – the report urges accelerated, collective and global action to get on an overshoot, peak and decline pathway. How quickly and strongly this action happens will define the shape and trajectory of the pathway.

Strong political will and multilateralism, effective policies, inclusive governance, and finance are all important enabling conditions for action – and equity and justice must underpin all responses. Countries with greater responsibility for climate change should act the fastest with the greatest ambition.

The report also finds that mitigation and adaptation, which are mutually reinforcing, must advance together, while being responsive to emerging risks. Interventions that achieve both mitigation and adaptation goals – such as nature-based cooling – should be prioritized.

Adaptation set up now forms the foundation for efforts to come, but it must become transformational and responsive to evolving non-linear and abruptly arising risks – including those that will harm mitigation efforts.

The report emphasizes that net-zero is a milestone towards net-negative, with CDR needed in addition to, not instead of, sustained reductions in greenhouse gas emissions. However, CDR can only contribute credibly to a return below 1.5°C if peak warming remains well below 2°C and all residual emissions are reduced. Strong governance frameworks for CDR will be critical to allow responsible deployment and manage implications for environmental integrity, equity, scale.

Years of inaction mean that even if a return to below 1.5°C is secured, irreversible losses and permanently changed conditions are certain. Many communities may be forced to relocate or change livelihoods, while societies will face the challenge of re-adjustment. This raises issues of justice, power, and political legitimacy, which will require new, inclusive governance arrangements to resolve difficult issues.

This report is a reminder that an overshoot, peak and decline pathway is a next generation climate frontier, but one which cannot be left unattended to for the next generation to tackle. Immediate action is required for such a pathway to remain possible.
